items.title: There are features in iPhone Duo that Apple didn't talk about
items.content_html:
Now that the iPhone Duo is at least partially out in the wild, the horde of reviewers that have used the device are finding things that were previously unannounced and undiscovered. Here are a few examples.

On September 9, Apple officially entered the folding smartphone market with its iPhone Duo. While customers won't be able to get their hands on one until October 23, select reviewers have already shared their thoughts on Apple's first foldable.

Alongside the usual opinions, many of these early reviews also detail obscure iPhone Duo features. For instance, when unfolded, the iPhone Duo supports Edge Light. In essence, the outermost area of the iPhone Duo's internal display acts as a ring light during FaceTime video calls.

This capability was previously exclusive to Macs with an Apple Silicon chip, which gained Edge Light with macOS Tahoe 26.2. This makes the iPhone Duo the first iPhone with Edge Light support. It's a nice touch for the foldable, but Edge Light is far from the only thing Apple customized for the iPhone Duo.

Because the iPhone Duo is similar in size to the iPad mini when unfolded, Apple opted to include a horizontal version of Reachability. Introduced in 2014, Reachability is an Accessibility feature that makes user interface elements near the top of an iPhone screen easier to access.

On the iPhone 6 and newer models, users can swipe down on the bottom edge of their iPhone screen to temporarily move the top of the iOS UI toward the lower half of the screen. This capability is available both on the iOS Home Screen and within applications.

With the iPhone Duo, the feature will seemingly work the same way, only with the left or right side of its displays. In essence, swiping towards the edge of the screen might move half of the on-screen UI to the left or right. Wired reports that the iPhone Duo will get reachability "later this year," per Apple.

Another capability launched with iPhone Duo is the Smart Take feature. Apple says the iPhone Duo "can detect when everyone is ready and takes the picture." This means no hassle with timers and no pushing buttons to take a picture with the iPhone Duo. It's also possible to use the outer display as a live viewfinder feed when taking photos.

Additionally, the iPhone Duo will gain Apple Pencil support with the upcoming iOS 27.2 update. The capability is already available with the release candidate build of iOS 27.2, which arrived on Monday.

However, while the iPhone Duo is undoubtedly full of useful product-specific UI enhancements, you'll only find them in Apple's apps, at least for the time being. Many third-party applications have yet to implement proper display support for the iPhone Duo's display aspect ratios.

As Engadget notes, many third-party apps viewed through the iPhone Duo's inner display only occupy the central area of the screen, leaving huge black bars on the right and left sides. Some applications, like Slack, however, have already addressed this issue.

Software-related details like these are eventually going to get fixed, but that won't be the case for the iPhone Duo's hardware. Some reviewers, like Arun Maini, have noted that desktop MagSafe chargers make the iPhone tip or rotate when the device is unfolded

Still, MagSafe is an entirely optional feature on the iPhone Duo. Apple's foldable can obviously be charged via USB-C, so the device won't tip over on its own. Overall, Apple still has a few kinks to work out with the iPhone Duo, and the product isn't for everyone, regardless of all the exclusive features it offers.

items.title: New PHP vulnerability means the Internet will have a very rough couple of days
items.content_html:
A severe vulnerability has been found in key web technology PHP, forcing just about everybody to patch websites, and fast. Expect outages.

Over the next couple of days, there will be more complaints about websites being down than usual. It's not just you, but the effects of the Internet relying on PHP and something going horrifically wrong.

The developers behind PHP, a web programming language, have said they will release a patch on Wednesday to fix a pair of vulnerabilities. They are rated at a very high 9.2 severity on the CVSSv4.0 severity scale.

The people behind the patch say that users should "upgrade as soon as the release is available," reports Reuters.

It is severe enough of a problem that EU cybersecurity officials have warned companies and organizations that can't apply the fixes must be prepared to take websites using PHP offline temporarily.

The EU Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) describes it as a risk of unauthenticated remote code execution. An attacker can insert code and run it on a vulnerable server.

The Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) has issued similar guidelines, advising to identify PHP servers and to apply patches, as well as to monitor for malicious activity.

While the ACSC wasn't aware of any active exploitation of the vulnerabilities, but Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said attacks were emerging. Cloudflare has updated its firewall rules as a temporary measure.

PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor or Personal Home Page) is a scripting language used in website development. It has been used for decades online, being one of the oldest technologies used to create interactive websites.

It is so popular that it has been used for many different platforms and purposes online, besides being used as a page scripting language.

Platforms including Drupal, Joomla, and Magneto heavily use PHP. So does WordPress, a blogging platform that is heavily used online by websites, including many that don't look like blogs.

In short, PHP runs many of the things that run the web, and this is a big problem.

This is a situation made worse by AI, which is being used to find vulnerabilities that hackers can exploit, or simply use AI to hack on their behalf.

End users do not have anything they can actually do about patching, unless they happen to have a personal web server using PHP. There are no patches needed for browsers or applications.

Really, all web users can do is hope that the patching and inevitable downtime don't take too long, and that the patches work.

You may want to keep a good book on standby to stave off boredom.

items.title: There will be extremely limited iPhone Duo stock in store on Friday
items.content_html:
Apple has confirmed that despite previous reports, Apple Stores will have a small quantity of iPhone Duo units for sale on October 23, 2026. Expect lines overnight.

First there was the incredibly fast selling out of the iPhone Duo during pre-orders, then there was Apple reportedly refusing to comment on in-store availability. But now an Apple spokesperson has said in a quite carefully phrased statement, that Apple Stores will have some.

Apple then also cautioned that it expects these limited stocks to sell out quickly. That's not a surprise, given the demand so far and the many previous reports of delays in iPhone Duo manufacturing.

The suggestion from Apple is that every store will have at least some stock. In AppleInsider's checking, it appears that every Apple Store is opening early on October 23.

That's at least likely to enable more time for pickup appointments from buyers who ordered online, however.

Apple does usually reserve stock so that stores have new iPhones on sale from the first day that pre-order buyers get theirs. But it usually manages to reserve sufficient quantities to serve walk-in customers and in this case it is at least extremely unlikely that it has managed to do so with the iPhone Duo.

After shipping dates slipped back almost instantaneously as pre-orders began, they appear to have now stabilized. Any pre-order placed now is listed as seeing a delivery date of January 25, 2027.

MacRumors first reported this statement.

items.title: Don't return an unexpected Apple Cash payment, it's a scam
items.content_html:
That Apple Cash payment you got from a stranger is not a mistake and the sob story they tell begging you to return it is just part of the con. Here's how to protect yourself.

You almost have to give scammers credit for ingenuity. Someone figured out how to profit from sending a stranger an iPhone, and now someone has found a way to manipulate Apple Cash users.

As happened to a Reddit user, the first thing is that you get an unexpected payment appearing on your iPhone in the Apple Cash part of Apple Wallet. It doesn't matter if you don't already use Apple Cash, as all that will happen is that you're prompted to set it up.

That setup prompt is Apple's and it is legitimate, because the payment appears to be too. If you're not expecting this payment and you haven't already setup Apple Cash, though, save yourself some time by declining the payment.

If you are a user already then by default, this payment will just go into your Apple Cash account. Then very shortly afterwards, if not immediately, you get a message asking you to please return it.

Doubtlessly, many people will just do that. If you hesitate even a little, the message ramps up the pressure.

First you're told it was a mistake, they meant to send it to someone else, but then they start getting really detailed.

Typically they'll say something about how the money was meant to go to something to do with their children. It'll have been for a basketball lesson or something, and if you still don't return the money, now you get sobbing emojis and a claim that it was the sender's last dime.

It's all to make you believe that returning the money is urgent, and so stop you having time to think about it.

What's really happening is that while, yes, you have received money, it was fraudulent. The issuing bank will eventually reverse the payment when, for instance, it's shown that it came from a stolen credit card.

So instead of a seemingly simple return of someone's cash, you will instead have paid them that cash out of your own money.

If you're reading this because it's currently happening to you, do not engage with the scammer's messages any further. Instead, try this first:

There won't be a Reject Payment button if you have already accepted the payment, though. And you may well have done that, as Apple Cash is set to automatically accept incoming payments from any source.

In that case, ignore or block any messages from this scammer and know that the payment will eventually vanish.

You can also turn off this automatic acceptance of payments to prevent this happening in future.

From then on, any time anyone sends you a payment, you will have to tap an Accept button to receive it. You'll have seven days in which to accept the payment.

This particular scam appears to be quite new, but the more people use digital wallets and digital payments, the more fraud attempts there will be. Most recently, scammers have been pretending Apple Pay payments have been declined, for instance.

items.title: iPhone Duo review roundup: Mostly positive opinions unfold
items.content_html:
The iPhone Duo is a big departure from the norm for Apple, and it's in the hands of critics. Here's what the first reviews say about the foldable smartphone.

The launch of the iPhone Duo has been a good one for Apple, with preorders selling out mere moments after they opened up on October 16. While many face long wait times and some confusion, deliveries for the lucky early buyers will start from October 23.

Of course, reviewers for tech publications and influencers have already got their hands on the new model, and have formed their own opinions about the release. After the lifting of a review embargo, those views are now being made public.

In general, the reviews are very favorable, with praise for the good features far outweighing the criticisms.

This is what the initial wave of reviews for the iPhone Duo say about the device.

The main thing that every reviewer focuses on is the iPhone Duo's party trick of having a large foldable internal 7.6-inch OLED with a nano-texture finish. Unlike the external 5.4-inch screen, the internal version is designed to be bent in the middle, closing the iPhone Duo like a book.

The iPhone Duo's massive display, unfolded.

Engadget refers to the screen as "glossy" and one that makes transitioning from one screen to another "super smooth" due to Apple's handling of the action. The matte nanotexture finish is seen as smart for cutting down on reflections and helping to hide the crease.

The YouTube review from MKBHD has similar praise for Apple's screen animations. He likens it to a lenticular sheet that slowly diffuses as it moves further away from the background.

CNET was most pleased by the fact that it "opens fully flat" and found that the larger display was used for tasks that required more time or effort. The cover display was very useful for less-involved tasks.

Typing is more comfortable on the inner display when rotated into a portrait orientation. In landscape, the keyboard felt "like a stretch" because of the extra width.

The design of the iPhone Duo is certainly welcomed by initial reviewers. TechRadar called the design "Apple at its best," even if it doesn't reinvent the foldable genre.

Side view of the iPhone Duo

While Apple is late to the folding party, Apple has landed on "the right shape," says Wired. The exterior display is still big enough to be useful, with the passport design feeling "better than what's come before in this category."

The design is "the right fit" for CNET, while Engadget enthuses about it having "one of the nicest hinges" the reviewer used on any foldable. Not only is it smooth, but it holds itself in a partially-open position while changing the pressure needed to unfold the device as it opens up.

As for whether Apple's hinge does the job well enough, Joanna Stern's New Things review involved the creation of a motorized folding machine, to repeatedly swing the hinge at 17 folds per minute.

Four nights and over 32,000 folds later, there was "no noticeable deterioration." The hinge did get a little stiffer after the experiment, but this too wasn't really noticeable in everyday use.

The selection of cameras Apple includes is also a major feature of its iPhones. However, the iPhone Duo has a dual-camera setup, not the triple-camera arrangement from the iPhone 18 Pro.

That means there's a pair of 48MP Fusion Main and Fusion Ultra Wide cameras, with the former also faking a 12MP 2x telephoto camera using a selective crop.

Rear cameras on the iPhone Duo

Engadget says the quality matches that of the Samsung Z Fold 8, with features like the exterior preview also liked. However, the best cameras in an iPhone are still in the iPhone 18 Pro.

In summarizing the iPhone Duo, reviewers provide the same sort of final thoughts. That Apple got it right with its first attempt at a foldable.

"The Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors," utters Wired. Engadget enthuses about its "exquisite design" that sidesteps the growing pains of a new class of gadget, because competitors went first.

CNET admits it's not for everyone, as not everyone needs a "phone that doubles as a tablet." Apple has managed to stick the landing, with hope that a telephoto camera and Face ID could arrive in a future update.

Stern summarized the Duo as one of the "most early-adopter Apple products" she tried in a long time. There's some trepidation in handing over $2,000 for the device, with the advice for some to "sit it out."

But there are clear indications that the future will be better, such as a lighter second-gen model with Face ID, better cameras, and time for software updates to fix some usability gripes.

To Tom's Guide, while the iPhone Duo is heavier and thicker than expected, it is the "foldable phone to beat" when it comes to design, the robust software experience, and durability.

items.title: Apple Music's gorgeous rebrand leans on Liquid Glass
items.content_html:
Apple has revealed how it used music itself to create the visuals for its new Apple Music rebrand that features a "made by sound" rippling visual sting.

First Apple remade its Apple Music logo into a more chunky design, then it unveiled a new visual identity at the opening of its Apple Music Hall in Battersea, London. Now in a new video, Apple has revealed how months of work went into the design.

"For the rebrand of Apple Music, we wanted sound to create the visuals," says the narrator of Apple's new video. "How do we take this idea of music and distill it into something visually beautiful? Essentially the idea was to create the perfect sound wave."

Apple Music partnered with British producer Fred Again... and NEST Acoustics to create a visual identity formed from sound.

"We take a frequency and we play it through a rig [which] then moves a large amount of liquid at the frequency of the notes," continues the narration. "We partnered with one of the world's best music artists to create the notes for the final mnemonic, and then we use that sound to create the visuals."

An Apple Music logo was etched into the glass floor of a small tank, and that was then filled with mineral oil. A transparent cover in the shape of an app icon was placed over the logo, and on the moving rig.

Then when a short series of tones, specially chosen for this work, were played, a transducer vibrated. It sends the oil rippling out from the rig and distorting the Apple Music logo.

That footage will now be used as a short sting introducing Apple Music videos. A version with just the two-note logo instead of any text is also to be overlaid at the start of Apple Music footage such as concert videos.

Both versions are very reminiscent of Apple's Liquid Glass redesign. Plus the fact that it was done in-camera with a practical effect instead of CGI is just as Apple did for its Apple TV rebrand in November 2025.

items.title: AI audio firm Samplab acquired by Apple to boost Logic Pro
items.content_html:
Apple has acquired AI audio editing firm Samplab, likely to extend Logic Pro's existing stem splitting tools, as well as adding the ability to edit individual notes in chords.

Following its deal with the Huxe AI podcast company, Apple has now acquired Zurich-based Samplab under a similar arrangement. As detailed in the European Union's public list of acquisitions, Apple is to acquire certain assets, and offer employment to certain Samplab employees.

Samplab was founded in Hauptsitz, Zurich, Switzerland, in 2020 by Manuel Fritsche and Gian-Marco Hutter. It's believed to have no more than 10 employees and based on LinkedIn profiles, may even only employ the two founders.

The company has previously described itself as being about "music production for the age of AI." Before being closed down, its official website promoted how its software could "change any note in your audio," and "detect and edit chords."

Samplab's software also included what the firm described as granular stem separation. Since 2024, Apple's Logic Pro has had stem splitting, which uses AI to isolate vocals, guitars, drums, and so on, into separate tracks.

The company's software was available as a plugin for Digital Audio Workstations (DAW), including Logic Pro. So while neither Samplab nor Apple have commented publicly, it seems most probable that the firm's technology will be used in Apple Creator Studio and Logic Pro.

Samplab's notice to existing users before its website was rerouted to Apple's - image credit: Samplab.

According to the EU, Apple made this deal through an unnamed subsidiary on June 17. In late June, Samplab's official website posted that it was closing down, and would be refunding subscribers with the remainder of their annual subscription fee.

That official site now routes through to apple.com. Other links to Samplab plugins are currently routing to a "page not found" on Apple's site.

Samplab's Twitter channel appears to have been gutted, and its YouTube channel has definitely had its videos removed.

This acquisition is the latest of several reported to the EU, with most being small firms such as Samplab, Huxe, and Prompt AI. It bought Q.Ai in January 2026 for an estimated $2 billion, however, and reportedly may be working to make other large-scale acquisitions.

items.title: Google Maps adds Gemini AI to CarPlay in U.S.
items.content_html:
Google Maps has added Gemini to CarPlay. Here's how you can access it.

Starting Wednesday, Google Maps users can access Gemini within CarPlay. This lets drivers and passengers ask Gemini questions using natural language.

For example, a driver can ask what the weather will be like at their destination when they arrive. They can also ask multi-step questions, such as where to stop for sightseeing and where to eat or get gas along the way.

To use it with CarPlay, users simply tap the Gemini icon in Google Maps on the infotainment system display.

This is the first time Google has made a voice assistant available within its CarPlay app. As 9to5Google notes, Google Assistant was only available when navigating directly from a user's phone.

Currently, the feature is limited to users within the U.S. Google plans to roll out the feature globally.

items.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for lying to users about privacy
items.content_html:
A New Mexico judge hit Meta with a record-breaking $25 billion penalty on Wednesday, stemming from a lawsuit over the Cambridge Analytica debacle.

The ruling follows September's guilty finding after a two-week trial. Ultimately, the court ruled that Meta was responsible for 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer privacy laws.

Each charge carried a penalty of up to $5000, leading to the record-breaking sum. Judge Francis J. Mathew of the Santa Fe State District Court made the ruling.

And this is on top of about $950 million in damages assessed earlier in the year after the state's judiciary found the social media giant liable for harms to children.

Also in 2026, the company negotiated a $17.1 billion settlement the company in August with 47 states, Washington DC, and other US territories. New Mexico led its own charge against the company and did not get involved in that case, nor its settlement.

The parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp has generated about $168.6 billion in profit over the trailing twelve months.

Meta's earnings are after the market closes on Wednesday, just hours after this announcement. The company has not replied to a request for comment from the New York Times yet, but it will certainly get asked some during that event.

Facebook has previously been fined $5 billion over the issue by the Federal Trade Commission.

Speaking in 2018, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that he had been "working to understand exactly what happened and how to make sure this doesn't happen again." Four years later, it's still not yet clear what the company has gleaned from the experience.

At around the same time, Apple's Tim Cook criticized the privacy failing, and said that it meant the time was past for companies to be allowed to entirely self-regulate.

"I think the best regulation is no regulation, is self-regulation," he said at the time, in answer to a question posed about Facebook. "However, I think we're beyond that here."

In 2023, there was a class-action payout from a $725 million settlement about the issue. The claim period is long past, and people in the US who used Facebook between May 24, 2007, and December 22, 2022, were eligible to receive a payment.

items.title: Apple blocks bafflingly weak internet security certificates on iPhone
items.content_html:
Apple has blocked on iOS and iPadOS a set of eight compromised security certificates that were found to be astoundingly weak. It's a bit more complicated on Mac.

Security certificates (SSL/TLS) are used to keep Internet users secure, thanks to using encryption to secure traffic and to verify domain ownership. However, a collection of certificates from one authority has been pulled from use after security researchers found them to be extremely weak.

As a result, Indian certificate authority eMudhra revoked the certificates. This prevents the certificates from being used by websites, closing the barn door after their discovery and disclosure on October 17.

According to Beeping Computer, Google Chrome blocked a set of six compromised intermediates authorized to issue TLS certificates. Meanwhile Mozilla blocked compromised certificates in Firefox.

While Google and Mozilla instigated the blocks on October 17, Apple was a little later in doing so. It added protections in iOS and iPadOS on October 19.

It's not so simple on Mac. More on that in a bit.

The point of a security certificate is that it can let systems identify each other and set up encryption between the two points. That encryption requires the creation of keys, both to set up and to decrypt the data.

This key is usually lengthy and complex, to a level that it would take way too much effort to guess the key or determine it by brute-forcing every possible combination, in a reasonable timeframe. Think along the lines of keys over 100 characters long.

In this instance, the keys for the eight certificates were entirely guessable, even by humans. The compromised private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

For clarity, those numbers aren't the lengths of keys. Those are the actual keys for each of the eight certificates.

This is on a par with using a system password of "password" or "123" and hoping it doesn't get guessed.

According to Mozilla's bug reporting system, Mozilla was able to recover the private keys very easily. And the keys were recovered without any prior knowledge of how the original reporter did it.

Of those eight certificates, six were used for TLS, and were trusted by Apple, Chrome, Microsoft, and Mozilla root programs. The other two are used for code signing and trusted by Microsoft.

Further complicating matters is that these certificates were generated in April 2025, so they have been available for well over a year. However, most of the certificates didn't make it into production, and there's no evidence of attackers recovering or using the keys either.

When it comes to what end users need to do, the advice is fairly simple: update your software as soon as you can. In some cases, like Mozilla's inclusion of the OneCRL system in Firefox, the protections were implemented without requiring a browser update or even a restart.

For Apple users, that means updating their apps, as well as iOS and macOS.

Mac users do still have to be wary, as the built-in curl utility doesn't check revocation information. If the Mac has encountered and trusted the certificates in the past, it will blindly continue to do so going forward.

That said, the assurance that most weren't use and the insistence that attackers haven't taken advantage of it may mean that few Mac users, if any, will be affected.

For eMudhra, in a statement on the matter, it insists there was no infrastructure compromise nor signs of any data breaches. It is also working with customers who may have been affected to replace the certificates.

items.title: Apple CEO John Ternus says design still means everything & includes whimsey
items.content_html:
"Design is how it works" rings true at Apple today, and John Ternus wants to assure everyone that respect for the user and building products that are beneficial is "job one."

John Ternus may be Apple's new CEO but he's not letting his new role interrupt his passion for industrial design. He emphasized that Apple had been working towards iPhone Duo for over 15 years in a previous interview.

A video version of that interview with Time was shared Tuesday with more conversation around the importance of design at Apple. Ternus starts by sharing his continued role of being involved with industrial design.

John Ternus joined Apple 25 years ago as a member of the product design team. His background in mechanical engineering placed him close to the industrial design team.

"I think what's so special about this place is design is at the center of it," Ternus shared. "Our designers both on the software side and the hardware side, they really understand the engineering. And the engineers have a deep appreciation for design."

"It's a really powerful collaboration," he concluded.

The conversation touched on similar topics in the previous published article, like child safety, Screen Time, and Ternus' love of driving fast cars. Everything centered around the announcement of the iPhone Duo and it representing Apple's ability to provide something useful while being whimsical.

"I think the opportunities in the products, that stuff will change," Ternus said in response to a question about Apple's future emphasis on design. "It'll evolve as it does as new technologies come, but the way we work — I don't want that to change."

Apple has notably sat out the larger portion of the AI race by not developing its own frontier model. Apple's executives have shared that the company doesn't need to develop everything, nor does it need to appeal to a "lunatic fringe."

"Design has always been at the core of this company, and I think our respect for the user and for building products that are helpful and beneficial to people — that is job one," Ternus concluded. "We're going to continue on that."

Apple ships the iPhone Duo to the lucky customers that managed to pre order one for release on October 23. The device has reportedly seen "extraordinary demand" and new orders won't ship until the end of January 2027.

items.title: Perplexity Computer can run completely local on Mac, with a big caveat
items.content_html:
Perplexity Computer now runs entirely on Apple Silicon Macs, but its recommended RAM requirement is pretty steep and limits actual deployments.

The fully local mode launched October 20 for Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. The release builds on April's Personal Computer launch and September's Hybrid Compute update. Personal Computer brought AI automation to native Mac apps, while Hybrid Compute paired local processing with cloud-based reasoning.

Users can now choose to keep an entire task on their Mac or authorize cloud processing when additional capabilities are needed. That is, assuming the minimum requirements are met.

The fully local version of Computer supports Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro, a Perplexity-trained version of Qwen. Both models run on the Mac, handling reasoning and coordinating tasks without relying on remote AI servers.

With permission, Computer can work across native apps including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers. Rather than simply generating text, the agent can collect information, modify documents, and complete tasks involving several apps.

Perplexity says Computer can review messages and emails, identify outstanding deadlines, and create a task list in Notes. It can also analyze private financial information against downloaded market data, update an Excel workbook, and prepare a Keynote presentation for review.

Code execution and tool operations take place in isolated sandbox environments, according to Perplexity, with controlled access to files and supported apps. Users can also authorize Computer to access cloud services for current information, browser use, connected apps, and advanced reasoning using more than 15 frontier models.

Fully local processing doesn't necessarily make every workflow independent of the internet. Sending an email or accessing an online service still requires a network connection, even when the AI model itself remains on the Mac.

Perplexity recommends at least 36 GB of unified memory for running Computer locally, which exceeds the maximum available in some recent Apple silicon Macs. According to Apple's technical specifications, the standard M6 Mac mini starts with 16 GB and supports a maximum of 32 GB, falling short of Perplexity's recommendation.

The M5 Pro Mac mini can meet the recommendation with a 48 GB or 64 GB configuration. Meanwhile, the M5 Max Mac Studio starts with 36 GB, making it the less expensive of the two Mac Studio configurations that meets the recommendation without upgrades.

Older Apple Silicon Macs with sufficient memory can also qualify. Perplexity describes 36 GB as a recommendation rather than a strict minimum, so users with less memory aren't necessarily prevented from running the software.

The recommendation illustrates how memory capacity can determine which Macs are suitable for demanding local AI workloads. Larger models need enough space for their data while leaving resources available for macOS and other running apps.

Perplexity previously published inference benchmarks for Qwen 3.6 on an M5 Max MacBook Pro. Those tests don't show how complete Computer workflows perform across different Mac configurations, and Perplexity hasn't released comparable results.

Perplexity's expansion comes as Apple moves to tighten macOS privacy protections against autonomous AI agents. On October 2, Apple announced plans to strengthen Full Disk Access controls to prevent apps from exposing sensitive information without users fully understanding the risks.

Full Disk Access allows backup utilities to reach files that macOS ordinarily protects, but it can also expose emails, messages, browsing history, and other private information. The risks extend to people communicating with the Mac's owner, whose information could become accessible through those apps.

In a developer notice, Apple said future controls will require more explicit user action before granting such extensive access. The company hasn't announced when those changes will arrive, and it isn't eliminating Full Disk Access entirely.

Perplexity says Computer uses controlled permissions and isolated execution environments, but its announcement doesn't specify whether the local agent requires Full Disk Access.

Local AI processing reduces the need to send private data to remote servers, but it doesn't eliminate security risks. An agent can still mishandle sensitive files or follow malicious instructions embedded in documents.

The launch also gives Mac users another alternative to Siri AI, which uses on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute infrastructure for more demanding requests. Both systems can work with personal context and perform actions across apps, although their capabilities and underlying architectures differ.

items.title: EU iPhone NFC concessions don't go far enough, says UK
items.content_html:
High fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions in the EU are said to be holding up wider third-party adoption of the NFC chip in an iPhone, and the UK is instead looking for easier access, and no cost.

Following both the UK's 2024 investigation into digital wallets, and Apple's agreement to open NFC access in Europe, the country's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) wants more. It argues that if Apple offers the same terms for UK developers, it will still be insufficient.

Consequently it wants easier access with fewer conditions. The CMA argues that none of this raises any security concerns, and that its proposals are needed to help UK businesses benefit from the technology.

"We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete," said Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA, in a statement. "By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services here — from payment apps and digital IDs to travel passes and digital keys."

The CMA notes that no firms have released an alternative to Apple Wallet in the UK, while five have in Europe. The first of those was Vipps, which launched in Norway in 2024.

According to the CMA, it is Apple's fees and access rules that are preventing rivals developing digital wallets. However, Apple has told AppleInsider and other venues that it disagrees with the UK's CMA.

"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections," said Apple in a statement. "We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

The CMA is currently presenting its proposals as a consultation. It is inviting comments until November 17, 2026, and says it will issue its decision shortly afterwards.

items.title: Apple still doesn't understand gamers in spite of iPhone being a gaming powerhouse
items.content_html:
An interview with the new App Store Worldwide head shows Apple is still playing by the same rulebook that fails to nail down what gamers want or need from a mobile platform.

If you've been following Apple long enough, you've heard this one before — Apple is finally serious about gaming. That's the mantra we've heard time and again from various product releases and Apple executives, but beyond financial success, it's hard to believe.

An interview conducted by Polygon with Apple's App Store Worldwide head Carson Oliver. The usual successes were listed, like having a Mac gaming app, powerful GPUs in Apple Silicon, and gaming-specific developer tools.

The thing is, Apple has always had a powerful platform for gaming on the iPhone. It is easily the most profitable gaming platform on Earth due to how many people own iPhones and pay for games.

However, very few gamers would consider iPhone, iPad, or especially Mac, a gaming platform. Sure, you can play games there, but they are the often derided "mobile" game.

Apple's previous attempts to address gamers have fallen flat, like the Apple Games app. Indie Games Week is the latest, and actually smart, move, but unless this is the start of a larger shift and not some one-time thing, nothing will change.

Today's mobile game is more advanced and beautifully rendered than ever. Call of Duty mobile's graphics rival previous-generation console shooters, while Genshin Impact feels like a game that shouldn't be able to exist on iPhone.

Some mobile games escape the stigma by being amazing experiences without the cruft

That is until you encounter your first loot box, gacha, or whatever scheme your game of choice is running.

Apple Arcade's promise was a great one that continues to shine through from time to time. Most of the games are direct ports of mobile games with ads and monetization stripped out.

The titles that stand out are the ones that could easily be found on a gaming console or in the Steam library. They're full games devoid of loot boxes or other schemes.

Yes, No Man's Sky is launching on iPhone and iPad in October, but that team already wanted to do that. Apple's technology made it possible, but I wouldn't herald this as some kind of victory or sign of more to come.

The interview shows a lot of contrasts and contradictions in Apple's game economy. Oliver touts iPhone's graphical prowess with the A20 Pro then mentions that the most popular games on the platform are indie titles that are predominantly pixel art.

Intensive graphics aren't a requirement to make a great game

"We've seen incredible growth of games coming to the App Store, in general, with more premium games releasing on the App Store this year than last," Oliver said. "While many of those are indies, we're also seeing more console and PC franchises coming to mobile, as it is a burgeoning audience for those games."

It sometimes feels like Apple is on the verge of getting it. Nintendo Switch has been so popular not because it's the most performant console on the market, but because its library is filled with fun and whimsical titles that don't need advanced GPUs to run.

He shares that popular games of the moment include Bolatro, Stardew Valley, Slay the Spire, and Bloons TD 6, which are all on Apple Arcade. That's nice and all, but I don't need an A20 Pro for those titles.

Gaming has seen a revival on iPhone thanks to Apple allowing emulators on the platform as well. However, Apple is shooting itself in the foot by not allowing more advanced emulators to run, like those that could emulate PlayStation 2 or Nintendo GameCube.

Apple's long history of gaming is filled with almosts and maybes. Every time it feels like they've figured it out, like with Angry Birds, Pokemon Go, and Infinity Blade, we end up with a race to the bottom.

There have even been multiple attempts to bring AAA games to iPhone, but they all fell flat. A lot of the reason behind these games flopping wasn't the price, execution, graphical fidelity, or anything relating to the games or hardware themselves.

'Death Stranding' works fine on iPad, but years late

The problem was, like many of Apple's efforts in gaming, too little too late with very little understanding of the gaming market. Those that wanted to play the Resident Evil 4 remake or Death Stranding already did years ago at full price on a console they owned.

What made matters worse is these games launched with an in-game purchase that was more expensive than what you could pay to get them on Steam or console. Many were even available as a part of a subscription like Xbox Game Pass or PlayStation Plus.

There's this movement in the gaming community asking for fewer games with worse graphics made by manageable team sizes that take longer to make a game. These ideals can be found in how much the gaming community latches onto indie darlings found on Steam.

'Cult of the Lamb' is a perfect example of what makes a great mobile game

Sure, there's always going to be a Grand Theft Auto VI or Elder Scrolls on the horizon that has everyone hyped. But, those games aren't on iPhone either.

Apple is trapped in this weird situation where it wants to be part of the conversation the way gaming consoles are, and wants a library as beloved as one on Steam, but it just never puts in the work. As has been exemplified again and again in the past decade, simply having game porting tools and powerful hardware isn't enough.

Game developers start with steam then port to consoles later. If a rare smartphone port happens, it's often a stripped-down version of the game filled with microtransactions or level selectors instead of linear storytelling.

My personal opinion is we need to get past "mobile," which demands addictive gameplay, monetization paths, microtransactions, and short gameplay loops. We also need to create a gaming platform on iPhone that can happily pay $7, $20, or even $60 for a title.

I'm serious. But make sure these games are available at full price at launch, not some years later when everyone has already played them elsewhere.

'Fantasian' proves that a full-length story-driven game can work on iPhone or iPad

The plague of "it has to be free then show loot boxes with premium passes" to succeed is killing us here. Stardew Valley is an amazing game because I can pay once, or get it on Apple Arcade, and play beginning to end without ever encountering an ad or microtransaction.

Fantasian, Hello Kitty Island Adventure, The Last Campfire, and plenty of others prove this is possible on iPhone. Embrace it, charge real money up front, and let me just play the game and get out of my way.

Sadly, Apple could never go that route because the cat is out of the bag. I'm afraid the only way that Apple can ever be serious about gaming is if it invents a time machine, goes back to when the App Store began, and encouraged game developers to charge real money for games.

There's a shift coming in the games industry thanks to AI-induced RAM and memory shortages. The PlayStation 6, if and when it ever releases, is estimated at over $1,000.

Games can survive generations regardless of graphic fidelity

It is making increasingly more sense to game on what you already own instead of investing in new hardware. Everyone owns a smartphone, and I expect we'll see a gaming-focused revolution on that front very soon.

The GameBoy, PlayStation Portable, and Nintendo DS were successful in spite of requiring specialized hardware to play expensive games that took upwards of 40 hours to complete. You can play many of those titles today thanks to emulation, which gaming companies seem allergic to finding a way to monetize.

My point is, your iPhone, iPad, and Mac are quite the capable gaming machines today. There are plenty of amazing titles you can play on them already, but Apple has an opportunity to make this a part of its brand.

Emulation lets us utilize existing hardware to explore classic games

Lean into it, find some developers and push to get their new pixel art-style game in the App Store. Promote one-time purchase games, rethink the App Store gaming page around what gamers actually want instead of what is most lucrative for Apple.

The real problem is Apple doesn't really need to change a thing, because regardless of gamer opinion on the matter, App Store games are among the most lucrative in the industry. It has to want to make a change for the better for gamers in spite of potential harm to revenue.

They're making money hand over fist because of mobile games preying on humanity's worst impulses. Gambling with loot boxes and paying to win are what define iPhone gaming, and unless Apple does something dramatic, it always will.

Let's see if Carson Oliver understands that and pushes Apple into finally getting serious about gaming. I wouldn't hold my breath.

items.title: iPhone camera and titanium chassis manufacturing expands in US
items.content_html:
Apple has announced new and extended partnerships with US firms to manufacture titanium for its iPhone enclosures and variable aperture technology for the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple's American Manufacturing Program (AMP) has already seen the company investing in firms across the country. One of those has been Qnity Electronics, and now Apple has announced that it is extending its partnership with this Delaware-based firm.

It's also revealed a new partnership with Pennsylvania's Perryman Company, a producer of titanium. Its titanium is to be used in the iPhone Duo and unspecified other devices.

"We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," said Sabih Khan, Apple's chief operating officer, in a statement. "American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro."

"We're proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support US jobs," he continued.

Apple says it will commit up to $100 million to the deal with Perryman over the next three years. The company melts, forges, and rolls titanium with a minimum of 80% recycled content for the iPhone Duo.

The expanded work with Qnity Electronics is said to specifically concern the new variable aperture camera now being used in the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple says that it now works with suppliers across all 50 states and that this supports over 450,000 American jobs.

This new announcement is a continuation of the initially $500 billion manufacturing investment announced in 2025. Apple has subsequently raised this figure to $600 billion, with the project set to run over four years.

Apple claims that almost 100 iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro components are being produced by companies in the US. These include long-time partner firms such as Corning, which is producing the iPhone's Ceramic Shield in Kentucky.

By the end of 2026, Corning's facility will reportedly be producing all of the cover glass for the iPhone and Apple Watch sold globally.

Then Apple CEO Tim Cook [middle] with Corning CEO Wendell Weeks [left] and CNBC's Jim Cramer [right] at Corning's facility in Kentucky - Image Credit: CNBC

As previously announced, Broadcom is expanding its radio frequency component production in Colorado. Coherent's Texas facility continues to provide components for Face ID and the Dynamic Island.

Then for processors, TSMC's Arizona fab is expected to produce over 100 million chips for Apple by the end of 2026. As TSMC continues to grow its Arizona campus, so Amkor Technology has begun construction for its packaging and test facility over in Peoria.

items.title: There's 4K 144Hz HDMI support in these new USB-C hubs for as little as $39.99
items.content_html:
Plugable has introduced two USB-C hubs starting at $39.99 that bring 4K 144Hz HDMI output to compatible Macs, offering high-refresh-rate monitor support without a larger docking station.

The new Plugable USBC-6IN1 costs $39.99, while the USBC-8IN1E costs $59.99. Both hubs support a single external display at up to 4K 144Hz or 8K 30Hz through HDMI 2.1.

They also offer USB-C pass-through charging and don't require drivers on macOS, Windows, or ChromeOS. Previously, Plugable offered 4K 144Hz output only in its more expensive USBC-10IN1E hub.

The new models bring that capability to smaller, more affordable accessories. Mac users still need compatible hardware and macOS 26 or later to achieve the advertised refresh rates.

The $39.99 USBC-6IN1 offers HDMI 2.1, three USB-A ports, and one USB-C data port. All four USB data ports support speeds up to 5Gbps, while the USB-C port and one USB-A port can deliver up to 7.5W of power to connected devices.

The aluminum hub measures 4.79 inches long and includes a built-in 6.7-inch USB-C cable. It provides the essential connections for a monitor and USB accessories without adding Ethernet or memory card readers.

The $59.99 USBC-8IN1E adds Gigabit Ethernet and separate SD and microSD card readers. Both readers support UHS-I speeds up to 104MB/s and can operate simultaneously, allowing photographers to transfer files from two cards without swapping them.

The $59.99 USBC-8IN1E adds Gigabit Ethernet and separate SD and microSD card readers.

The USBC-8IN1E also includes a 5Gbps USB-C data port, a 5Gbps USB-A port, and a USB 2.0 port intended for wireless keyboard and mouse receivers. It measures 5.99 inches long and uses the same 6.7-inch integrated cable.

Both hubs support up to 100W of USB-C Power Delivery input, with a maximum of 85W passed through to the connected laptop. The remaining 15W is reserved for the hub and its ports, and neither model requires an external power adapter for basic operation.

Achieving 4K 144Hz or 8K 30Hz requires a Mac running macOS 26 or later with an M1 or M2 Pro or Max chip, or an M3 chip or newer. Users also need a compatible monitor and HDMI 2.1 cable.

Base M1 and M2 MacBooks, along with the MacBook Neo, are limited to 4K 60Hz through these hubs. Windows laptops require DisplayPort 1.4 with Display Stream Compression to reach the higher resolutions and refresh rates, while systems using DisplayPort 1.2 are limited to 4K 60Hz.

Each hub provides one HDMI output and doesn't increase the number of external displays a Mac can natively support.

Plugable lists the USBC-6IN1 and USBC-8IN1E for $39.99 and $59.99, respectively, with availability beginning October 20 through Amazon and Plugable's website. The company also advertises a 20% launch discount.

items.title: OLED iPad mini and touchscreen MacBook Pro: What to expect from Apple's second October event
items.content_html:
Apple has another release event, and this one is called "Pro and Tell." This is what will make an appearance on the day, including one very long-awaited MacBook Pro upgrade.

Fall has been unusually busy for Apple in 2026. After surprise Mac launches in late August and the usual September iPhone event, it's also launched smart home products in October.

But it's far from done. There's still more for it to launch.

Apple will hold the event on October 28. This would be the second event in the same month, making it one of the most intensive product-launch periods on record.

The event was confirmed by messages to invitees to an event called "Pro and tell." The name all but confirms changes to the MacBook Pro are on the way.

The invitation also includes an Apple logo, in what could be best described as an outline of a radar sweep. The colors used by the lines on the dark background are reminiscent of the MacBook Pro's usual colorways.

Can't wait to pro and tell next week. https://t.co/3wUkxwq35i

Greg Joswiak, aka "Joz," the SVP of Worldwide Marketing, also posted the logo to X, saying "Can't wait to pro and tell next week."

On when to expect to be able to get your hands on whatever Apple launches, a store refresh planned for November 6 may indicate when sales commence.

Entering the fall, Apple had a massive catalog of potential launches on its hands. A multi-launch slate of products was anticipated.

That has so far included the Mac mini and Mac Studio updates in August as an early surprise launch.

Apple launched a lot during its September 9 "Surprise and Shine" event, including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and the fifth-generation AirPods.

The first October event was all about the smart home, with updates made to the Apple TV 4K and the HomePod mini 2. There was also the introduction of the HomeView and a bunch of related smart home device launches to match.

That sheer quantity of product launches is enough for any normal year, but there are still some candidates for launch. That launched items list doesn't have any iPad products, nor does it include any portable Mac models, which are now expected for this new event.

iPad mini

Back in September, it had a good chance of launching alongside the iPhones, but the iPad mini update is still expected to arrive. Based on the current state of rumors that would be the late October event.

One way of knowing it's on the way is from a French regulatory website. An identifier was found that related to the iPad mini, practically confirming the model's imminent arrival.

The eighth-generation device's main change is anticipated to be the display. An 8.4-inch LTPS panel with hybrid OLED should bring it in line with the iPad Pro range, if not to the same standard of specifications.

While brighter and more vibrant, the display won't necessarily have ProMotion, typically a Pro model feature. However, as usual for the rumor mill, that is still up for debate.

iPad mini on an arm

Beyond the display, you can also count on a chip upgrade. The current favorite is the A20, along with the possible inclusion of Apple's networking and modem chips.

Smaller changes that have been rumored include a repositioning of the FaceTime camera, as well as a new vibration-based speaker to help improve water resistance.

OLED MacBook Pro

One of the big-hitter rumors for the MacBook Pro line has been the display. An OLED-equipped model has been rumored a long time, and it seems like it'll finally arrive.

Forecasts previously put a launch at early 2027, but it's now thought to take place in October. Or at least to be announced in October with a release in November.

That seems to match the late event rumors quite well.

An OLED display produces a more vibrant image with high levels of contrast, while also saving power. As a touchscreen, it will also be the first MacBook to be touch-enabled, and join a notebook market that already has many touch-enabled displays.

On October 5, references were found in the macOS 27.2 developer beta, indicating multiple applications were set up to receive additional touch recognition capabilities. This is probably an inadvertent confirmation from Apple that it's on the way.

You can probably expect it to be a spec-bump update beyond the display, including using Apple's newer chips.

There may be a change in construction that helps it lose weight. On October 4, a report claimed there will be a significant weight reduction, thanks to Apple redesigning components to be smaller and lighter.

However, an October 8 report walked back earlier claims that there would be a chassis upgrade that made it thinner.

M6 MacBook Pro and iMac

Following the surprise launches of the M6 Mac mini and updated Mac Studio in late August, the prospect of spec-bump updates to other Mac models was good. While everyone will be looking at the new OLED model, other entry-level models are still a possibility.

The most obvious ones that have been rumored about are the M6 models. There are M6 models of MacBook Pro and iMac allegedly on the horizon, catching up to the M6 Mac mini.

The current 24-inch iMac.

The entry-level M6 MacBook Pro rumors say that it will still use a mini LED screen with ProMotion. It'll also use an identical six-speaker sound system, the same ports, and the same chassis as the current generation.

However, it will instead get an upgrade to the M6 chip, making it a typical Apple spec-bump upgrade.

It's a similar story for the M6 24-inch iMac, with it also thought to be given a speed boost, but retain the current design. An overhaul with OLED is expected for the iMac at some point, but that will be far into the future.

For now, any iMac upgrade will keep the display as-is.

What appears above is what we expect Apple to show during the late October event. There's even more waiting in the wings, but they're rumored to be arriving at a later time, in early 2027.

That list includes updates to:

As always, AppleInsider will keep tabs on the rumor mill and potential launches in the future.

items.title: Taction won record-breaking $5.7 billion verdict against Apple, asks for more
items.content_html:
Taction hopes that the court will award additional damages for iPhone and Apple Watch sales made in 2026 in addition to hundreds of millions in prejudgment interest.

Even as Apple challenges the $5.7 billion verdict set by a jury in the Taction patent case, the company hopes to squeeze out more. A jury ruled that Apple violated two patents, though not willingly, and Apple denied any wrongdoing.

According to a report from Reuters, Taction has asked a federal judge for hundreds of millions more in payment from Apple. It argues that the damages only cover from 2021 to March 2026 and should cover the previous six months as well.

Taction has also asked for prejudgment interest at California's 7% statutory rate. The interest on $5.7 billion would be an incredible figure on top of the already large sum.

The argument is simple. Taction says "the size of the jury's award is no reason to withhold interest."

Of course, Apple plans to appeal and has already challenged the jury's verdict. It was allegedly made without any materials to accurately determine the damages payment.

Plus, the logic of the case and the alleged infringement are contradictory. Apple hopes it can have the whole thing thrown out with a summary judgment, but no verdict has been shared yet.

items.title: HomePod mini 2's Sound Glow feature is coming to other HomePod models
items.content_html:
With the tvOS 27.2 and HomePod Software 27.2 release candidates, Apple has added support for surround sound on the 2026 Apple TV 4K and for Sound Glow on select HomePods.

On October 13, as part of its "Welcome Home" event, Apple's streaming box and smallest smart speaker received meaningful hardware upgrades. A new surround sound option is also available when you pair the latest Apple TV 4K with four HomePod mini 2 units.

Alternatively, it's also possible to use four HomePod 2 speakers, or two HomePod mini 2 units and a pair of HomePod 2 speakers for the surround sound experience. Owners of the original HomePod mini and HomePod are out of luck, though cheaper, better-sounding surround sound alternatives are available.

With the tvOS 27.2 release candidate build, deployed on Monday, Apple included code related to its new surround sound feature. The company did so even though the new-and-improved Apple TV 4K won't be in users' hands before November 13.

Priced at $300, the 2026 Apple TV 4K offers a more powerful A19 chip, support for Siri AI, and far-field microphones for echo cancellation. At its core, though, the device is just a streaming box, and it's increasingly difficult to justify buying one.

Meanwhile, the HomePod Software 27.2 release candidate extends Apple's new Sound Glow feature to the HomePod 2 and original HomePod mini. With Sound Glow, the top of compatible HomePod models pulses colors that match the audio being played.

It's a neat visual detail, but nothing groundbreaking. The key selling points of HomePod mini 2 include Siri AI support and the new surround sound feature for Apple TV.

items.title: Simplicity and Siri AI are the HomeView's killer features, says Apple
items.content_html:
The new Siri AI is the "magic" of HomeView, according to Apple execs, but part of that is how little users should have to interact with it.

HomeView is Apple's new $299 home hub device, and it was long rumored to be ready but waiting for Siri AI. Now that both that and the hardware are out, Apple has been stressing just how significant Siri AI is.

"With the magic of Siri AI, [HomeView] comes together in a way that we haven't been able to deliver before," Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home, told The Verge in a new interview.

That "magic" concerns in part how Siri AI has a more conversational understanding of how people speak. Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple, said that it's "great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way."

"As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way," she continued. "Because now it can be my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who's in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want."

Another part of Siri AI that is important yet doesn't get enough recognition is that it doesn't converse for the sake of it. Siri AI may be more conversational, but it is there to do a job for you.

"A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information," continued Rincon. "For us, it isn't about that. We're there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way."

Rincon leads product marketing and management for Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. She joined Apple from Google in March 2026.

Apple makes a persuasive case for how the HomeView avoids complexity, and doesn't try to be some kind of AI companion. HomeView has been designed for a particular type of user, or perhaps for the family of the right user.

Since it doesn't actually ship until November 13, 2026, there is still much to find out. But already the HomeView's limitations, intentional or not, are becoming apparent.

The chief one is that the screen is very small, especially for something Apple says can be wall mounted like a clock at the end of your kitchen. But then there is the fact that no apps can be run on HomeView, and so for common features like watching Apple TV, you have to AirPlay from your iPhone.

It's not clear that this element will ever be changed. But Apple is already reported to be working on a HomeView with a larger display.

items.title: Apple's latest design showcase explores how furniture can inspire us to stay present
items.content_html:
Apple's latest design showcase uses familiar objects to explore how people connect with their surroundings and each other.

Apple's second Designers of Tomorrow showcase brings four emerging design practices to Design Miami Paris. This year's Design for Presence theme explores how physical objects encourage attention, reflection, and interaction.

Curator Rodman Primack heads the exhibition, which Wallpaper* previewed ahead of its opening. Participants used Apple tools, including iPad, Apple Pencil, and MacBook Pro, to develop their work.

Image credit: Apple

Egyptian-Danish architect Salem S. Charabi created "The Eminence of Light" using materials found around his Cairo studio. The lantern combines a limestone base, a banana paper diffuser, and interlocking date palm fronds.

"For this project, every component had to be mapped out in detail. I sketched and did all the 3D modelling on my MacBook Pro. It was a complex process getting everything to fit just right — from the carving of the stone and the paper moulds, down to the delicate base."

Brooklyn designer Isabel Rower based "The Padded Chair 1860" on a historic chair she photographed in Paris. Its fringe contains over 1,500 ceramic beads, designed to produce an appealing sound when brushed.

"A few years ago I took a photograph of a boudoir chair from the 1860s in the Musee des Arts Decoratifs in Paris. I found the form highly unconventional and I was drawn to its dramatic fringed skirt. When faced with the prompt of 'Design for Presence', I felt that this chair was the perfect object to revisit."

Seoul artist Yoonjeong Lee's "New Form" combines a wooden table with an integrated lamp. Roughly 5,000 veneer sheets form its base, while three worn pencils secure the paper lampshade.

"One day, I was looking at a pencil that was almost used up, and I noticed its shape looked like a nail," she told Wallpaper*. "A pencil doesn't disappear as it wears down. It stays on in a new form: as a letter, as knowledge, as music. For me, it stayed on as a nail."

Mexican studio Parafernalia developed "MonoAmbiente 1", a folding table with two stools that nest beneath it. Its acid-etched stainless steel surfaces form a continuous landscape when the furniture is closed.

"Conversation is rarely an isolated activity. We talk while we play, eat, drink, walk, or cook. In this piece, the accompanying activities create the conditions for dialogue rather than defining it," the designers said of the piece. "The deployment of the piece marks a shift from solitary observation to shared occupation, from looking to participating."

The exhibition runs October 21 through October 25, 2026, at Hotel de Maisons in Paris.

items.title: Release candidates of iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 land as release nears
items.content_html:
The first release candidates for iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, and macOS 27.2 have arrived for testing.

The first release candidates for iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, and HomePod Software 27.2 have surfaced, following four developer beta cycles, three for tvOS 27.2 and HomePod Software 27.2.

While a release candidate or RC version means the update is practically at the state it will be distributed to the general public, there's no guarantee it will be the only one. A second RC is always a possibility.

The first major post-milestone update is normally a point-one version, which unusually isn't the case this time. As the iOS 27.1 build is designated to be used with the iPhone Duo, that version is being skipped for the non-foldable iPhone models.

The new 27.2 builds are:

Apple has also released RC builds for older operating systems:

The RC round arrives after the fourth developer betas, which were distributed on October 5. However, while there were builds for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and visionOS, the round didn't include builds for tvOS nor HomePod Software.

The third round was shared by Apple on October 5. The second appeared on September 21, and the first round landed on September 16.

The first round introduced a few changes to iOS 27.2, including a redesigned Health app, which works alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12.

FaceTime gained dual capture support, Siri AI added localization for multiple languages, and Apple TV profiles from tvOS 26.2 came over to the iPhone.

The second build had indications of a new AutoLock security feature, which locks down an iPhone if it is detected to have been snatched or otherwise stolen from the owner. The feature isn't accessible to testers, but it was spotted as running in the background in a non-functional manner.

The fourth iOS 27.2 beta had Apple Music change its icon to black and white, as well as a withdrawal of the redesign of the Apple Health app in favor of a later release. HomePods also gained a new setting to Lock Controls.

AppleInsider warns readers trying out beta software should do so on secondary, spare hardware instead of their mission-critical or daily driver devices. There is always a risk of buggy, broken, or other potentially harmful elements in beta software, which can be a risk to your data.

items.title: Jason Sudeikis holds out hope for more 'Ted Lasso'
items.content_html:
"Ted Lasso" star and co-creator Jason Sudeikis says that he doesn't know if the show will continue, but he wants it to and assumes Apple TV does too.

It took three years for Apple to revive "Ted Lasso," and that was despite then-CEO Tim Cook himself wanting more. Now with the fourth season finished, Jason Sudeikis has said he hopes for more.

Speaking on the podcast "Talk Easy with Sam Frogoso," Sudeikis said that the idea of reviving the show at all was to do more than one new run. "I mean, that was the endeavor of going back into it," he said, "just sort of like, oh, I think there's more in there."

"I would like to [do more], yeah, I think it would be fun," he said. "I just don't know. We haven't started a writers' room or anything like that."

But asked if Apple would do more so long as he wanted to keep doing it, Sudeikis said "I would assume so."

The odds of a fifth season are already high, though, because of how Apple TV tends to commission two seasons at a time. That's common practice in television for contractual reasons, but it can also be that a streamer will cancel a show rather than take up the option for the next run.

That normally happens when a show fails to perform, and while Apple has not released official figures, "Ted Lasso" season four is estimated to have attracted nearly 300 million US viewing minutes in its first two days. There were previous reports of the production having been problematic, though.

Reports in July 2026 said that production ran a month behind schedule. It was also said that problems had resulted in what were called "come to Jesus" Zoom calls between the production team and Apple TV.

Previously, television producers have told AppleInsider off the record that Apple TV is hands-off so long as it likes the footage it's seeing and there are no problems. If Apple decides it needs to step in on a production, however, the chances of further seasons are nil.

Back in July, Sudeikis said that he intended to get a writers' room together for a fifth and perhaps sixth season by August. That apparently hasn't happened yet, but Sudeikis could well now be contractually bound not to say so.

items.title: Check your iPhone Duo shipment date, it may have moved up
items.content_html:
As it typically goes, iPhone Duo buyers who had orders after release day may get their order earlier than expected. But, in one country, that may not be the case.

Just like other popular Apple products, preorders for the iPhone Duo sold out within moments of opening. It only took a short while for consumers to see delivery dates go further into the future, before stabilizing to late January.

The high demand means there's no chance of simply walking into an Apple Store and buying one on launch day. But, if social media posts are to be believed, it may not be the three-month wait that consumers currently expect to receive their orders.

On X, some users are claiming to see their shipment dates for the iPhone Duo to be a lot sooner.

One posted on Sunday that their pre-order status through T-Mobile has an estimated ship date ship date of October 22. Based on a typical next-day delivery for such orders, that would mean an arrival on October 23, the launch date.

It's not a change that all users will see, and probably not as close as launch day itself. And in that case, stock is drawn from T-Mobile's, not Apple's.

Even so, Apple has a history of under-promising and over-delivering iPhone orders.

While earlier release dates are good news for iPhone Duo buyers, it is best to double-check that it is correct. There is a possibility that this is a big mistake.

Posting to X, Gizmodo's Ray Wong claims his X feed is full of Japanese users saying their preorders have shifted to arrive on October 23. This would be a change from previous dates claiming deliveries in November and December.

In some cases, users are allegedly seeing launch day deliveries, despite ordering on Monday.

A social media poster apparently "confirmed" with Apple that it was a system error, and that the launch day changes were incorrect. That said, Wong believes it may have been a discussion with a person at an Apple Store rather than Apple corporate, putting the claim into question.

If it is an Apple issue, then you can expect a wave of responses from those same social media users as their dates get corrected.

As it stands, there's still a bit of a wait before eager customers get their hands on the iPhone Duo. It just may be a shorter wait than some anticipated.
